definition: Restitution is a form of redress in law that restores what was lost through a violation of rights, rather than paying for the injury in some other way. In the source, it is contrasted with compensation as one way of remedying harm already suffered.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Action (law); pinned source text

reasons: The packet only says that redress may be secured sometimes through restitution and sometimes through compensation; it does not define restitution as restoring what was lost through a violation of rights.
The definition adds an explanatory contrast and mechanism for restitution that are not stated in the source text, so the substantive sense is too specific for the supplied evidence.
The packet does not define “restitution”; it only mentions the term in passing within the description of “Redress” for an “Action (in law).”
The definition’s specific claim that restitution “restores what was lost through a violation of rights” is not supported by the packet text.
While the packet does support a contrast between “restitution” and “compensation,” the added elaborations in the definition are unsupported.
